```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from _study import (SALES, EVAL_ROSTER, WINDOWS, VALIDATION_ORIGIN,
                    scored, table_of, rename_models, md, metrics, plots, pl)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
```

A foundation model is only impressive against something. So I began by building the reference
it would have to beat: a feature-engineered gradient-boosting model, in the tradition that
won M5, inspired by a public top-4% solution.

The result worth stating up front is how little those 52 engineered features buy over the
mean of the last 28 days. That is not a criticism of the solution I reproduced — I reduced it
to a single XGBoost model where the original used LightGBM — but it is what makes the
comparison in [the next post](../02-chronos2/) far more interesting.

## The dataset

One target value per series per day: units of one item sold in one Walmart store. History
runs 2011-01-29 to 2016-05-22, 1,941 days, 30,490 series. I work throughout on a frozen
random sample of 500 series, drawn once and saved, so every number in these three posts comes
from the same items. The sample is for tractability, nothing more.

```{python}
#| label: fig-intermittency
#| fig-cap: "Left: share of on-sale days with no sale, one count per series. Right: mean units sold per day, log scale, by product category. The population I forecast is mostly near zero."
#| code-fold: true
on_sale = SALES.filter(~pl.col("is_missing"))
per_series = on_sale.group_by("id", "cat_id").agg(
    pl.col("sales").mean().alias("mean_daily"),
    (pl.col("sales") == 0).mean().alias("zero_share"),
)
median_zero = per_series["zero_share"].median()
median_daily = per_series["mean_daily"].median()

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2))
left.hist(per_series["zero_share"].to_numpy(), bins=np.linspace(0, 1, 21),
          color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, edgecolor="white")
left.set_xlabel("share of on-sale days with zero sales")
left.set_ylabel("number of series")
for category, colour in plots.CATEGORY_COLORS.items():
    values = per_series.filter(pl.col("cat_id") == category)["mean_daily"].to_numpy()
    right.hist(values, bins=np.logspace(-2, 2.5, 28), histtype="step",
               linewidth=2, color=colour, label=category)
right.set_xscale("log")
right.set_xlabel("mean units sold per day (log scale)")
right.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The median series sells `{python} f"{median_daily:.2f}"` units a day and is silent on
`{python} f"{median_zero:.0%}"` of the days it is on the shelf. Two consequences run through
everything that follows.

First, **a zero is usually information, not a gap.** The one exception is structural: days
before an item's first price in `sell_prices.csv`, when it was not on the shelf at all.
Those are dropped from every history. Everything else is a real zero — the item was
available and nobody bought it — and it is part of what the forecast has to get right.

Second, **the evaluation metric over a period of zero sales cannot be a percentage error.**
Dividing by an actual of zero is undefined, and most actuals are zero.

## The harness comes first

I set two forecast origins:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-windows
#| tbl-cap: "The two windows. Every choice I make is made on the validation window; I read the test window once, at the end of the next post."
#| echo: false
md(WINDOWS)
```

A (series, window) pair is scored only if it clears three conditions: at least 56 days
(arbitrary, but reasonable) on sale before the origin, no missing day inside the window, and
at least one unit sold in the window. The third is necessary — WMAPE and WQL divide by the
window's total, so a series that sells nothing has no defined error.

What matters more than the conditions is that **I report the count each one removes
separately**, and that the surviving list is frozen to disk. A roster that quietly changes
between models turns every later comparison into a comparison of populations.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-roster
#| tbl-cap: "Scored series per window, from the frozen evaluation roster."
#| code-fold: true
md(EVAL_ROSTER.group_by("role").agg(pl.len().alias("scored pairs"),
                                    pl.col("id").n_unique().alias("series")))
```

Of the 500 sampled series, 473 are scorable on the validation window and 485 on the test
window. In both cases every exclusion is the no-sale condition: none of the 500 is short of
history, and none has a missing day inside either window.

### Five metrics, and what each is for

| metric | definition | what it is for |
|---|---|---|
| MAE | mean of $\lvert y - \hat y\rvert$ | error in units sold |
| WMAPE | $100 \cdot \sum \lvert y - \hat y\rvert / \sum y$ | scale-free, survives zeros: the headline |
| P90 | 90th percentile of $\lvert y - \hat y\rvert$ | the bad days |
| WQL | mean over $q \in \{0.1,\dots,0.9\}$ of $2 \sum L_q / \sum y$ | the whole forecast distribution |
| RQL | $100 \cdot \sum L_{0.2}(y, \hat y) / \sum y$ | the point forecast, with over-prediction priced at four times under-prediction |

$L_q$ is the quantile loss on a forecast $f$: $q\,(y - f)$ when $f$ is too low,
$(1-q)(f - y)$ when it is too high. WQL applies it to each quantile forecast $\hat y_q$ in
turn, which is where it is a proper scoring rule — minimised by reporting the true quantile.
RQL applies $L_{0.2}$ to the point forecast $\hat y$ instead, because the asymmetry is meant
to price the cost of acting on the number the model puts forward. Scoring it on the 0.2
quantile column would reward a model for submitting a deliberately low number: on this data
that is worth a factor of about 2.8 at identical forecasting skill. All sums run over scored
(series, day) pairs, never averaged per series and then averaged again.

One identity decides how the next post must be read: **for a model that only gives a point
forecast, every quantile column is a copy of it, and WQL collapses to WMAPE/100.** A
probabilistic model can beat that number only by saying something true about its own
uncertainty. So WQL is not a fair axis for comparing a point model with a distributional
one; MAE, WMAPE, P90 and RQL are.

I check the metric code against three cases whose answers are known in advance: a perfect
forecast scores 0 everywhere; a constant zero forecast scores WMAPE 100, WQL 1 and RQL 20;
and a point forecast's WQL equals its WMAPE/100.

## Three naive baselines

Always zero, repeat-last-week, and the mean of the last 28 days. On intermittent data the
first is not absurd, and the third is a genuinely strong competitor — which is exactly why
it is here.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-baselines
#| tbl-cap: "Validation window. Lower is better everywhere."
#| code-fold: true
baselines = ["zero", "seasonal_naive", "moving_average_28d"]
md(rename_models(table_of(baselines, "validation"))
   .select(["model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("WMAPE"))
```

Note the ordering: repeating last week is barely better than predicting nothing at all,
while a flat 28-day mean removes about a fifth of the error. On series this sparse the
weekly pattern of a single item is mostly noise, and averaging it away beats reproducing it.

RQL inverts the ranking — the zero forecast wins it outright, 20 against 39. That is the
metric doing its job, showing how low volume the real values mostly are.

## The features

Rather than invent a feature set, I reproduced one that is public and placed well:
[btrotta/kaggle-m5](https://github.com/btrotta/kaggle-m5) (`predict.py`), a top-4% M5
solution. Fifty-two features in four families:

- **the series' own past** — lags 1 to 7, means of the last 7/14/28 days, running mean and
  variance overall and per weekday;
- **the same, two levels up** — the item's department in its store, and the item across all
  stores, so a thin series borrows the shape of its neighbours;
- **calendar** — weekday, month, SNAP benefit days, and an "event uplift" measured as mean
  sales *n* days after an event minus the same weekday a week later;
- **price** — the current price and its change over 7 and 14 days, plus days since first sale.

The strategy is **direct**: 28 models, one per forecast day. The model for day *k* sees
sales only up to the origin, with its lag features shifted *k* days further back, so no
forecast is ever fed back as an input and nothing in the window leaks.

Five differences from the original are deliberate:

- XGBoost instead of LightGBM, with the closest equivalent settings;
- **training on the 500-series sample** rather than all 30,490 — though the department and
  item features are still computed on all of them;
- boosting rounds chosen by early stopping on the last 28 days *before* the origin, where
  the original stops on the window it then reports;
- the event uplift implemented as intended rather than as coded;
- missing days defined by the price file.

The second and third cost real accuracy, and I kept them anyway: a reproduction that scored
*better* than the original would be the suspicious outcome.

## What it buys

```{python}
#| label: tbl-xgb
#| tbl-cap: "XGBoost against the baselines, both windows."
#| code-fold: true
models = baselines + ["xgboost_btrotta"]
md(rename_models(pl.concat([
    table_of(models, role).with_columns(pl.lit(role).alias("window"))
    for role in ("validation", "test")
])).select(["window", "model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("window", "WMAPE"))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-buckets
#| fig-cap: "Validation window, by horizon bucket. Baselines in grey. The gap to the 28-day mean opens only in the second fortnight."
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plots.plot_by_bucket(table_of(models, "validation", by="horizon_bucket"),
                                 metrics.METRICS)
plt.show()
```

Fifty-two features, 28 trained models and roughly 84 minutes of CPU at the test origin,
against a flat mean of the last 28 days: **0.8 WMAPE points on validation, 1.2 on test.**
The horizon view says where that comes from — the two are nearly tied over the second
week, then the mean decays while the model does not, which is the one thing a model
with a calendar in it ought to manage. The first week is to the model's advantage too.

The per-series view is blunter still.

```{python}
#| label: fig-index
#| fig-cap: "Per-series difference in WQL, XGBoost against the 28-day mean, series ordered by sales volume in the window."
#| code-fold: true
def per_series_wql(model):
    return metrics.score(scored(model, "validation"), by="id").select(
        "id", pl.col("WQL").alias(f"WQL_{model}"))

volume = (scored("xgboost_btrotta", "validation")
          .group_by("id").agg(pl.col("y").sum().alias("volume")))
comparison = (per_series_wql("moving_average_28d")
              .join(per_series_wql("xgboost_btrotta"), on="id")
              .join(volume, on="id"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
share = plots.index_plot(ax, comparison, "WQL",
                         "moving_average_28d", "xgboost_btrotta", order_by="volume")
plt.show()
```

XGBoost has the lower WQL on `{python} f"{share:.0%}"` of series. It loses on the majority
of items and still wins overall, because the items it wins on are the ones that sell. Pooled
metrics weight by volume; a per-series count does not. Both numbers are true, and quoting
only the pooled one is exactly the kind of claim I built this harness to catch.

## What the baseline settles

Three things carry into the next post.

**A number to beat.** WMAPE 78.8 on validation, 76.4 on test — and the honest framing is
that most of that was already available from a 28-day mean.

**An axis on which to beat it.** XGBoost returns a point forecast, so the comparison is MAE,
WMAPE and P90. Its WQL is arithmetic, not a measurement.

**A caveat that cuts the other way.** XGBoost is trained on squared error, so it estimates a
conditional mean. On absolute-error metrics the optimal point forecast is the *median*, so
any model that returns a median starts with a structural advantage on MAE and WMAPE that has
nothing to do with forecasting better. Chronos-2 returns a median, so in case of a tight
match strong conclusions could be risky.
